entities.name: Lancelotto Malocello
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lancelotto Malocello, a Genoese navigator and merchant, emerged as a pivotal figure in the early 14th century's nascent European engagement with the Atlantic, predating the more celebrated Iberian voyages of the Age of Exploration. His confirmed voyage to the Canary Islands around 1312 marked a significant, albeit temporary, re-establishment of European presence in an archipelago known to classical antiquity but largely forgotten in the Latin West. Malocello's expedition underscores Genoa's formidable maritime capabilities and commercial ambitions beyond the Mediterranean, positioning him as a critical, if often overlooked, bridge between medieval trade networks and the burgeoning Atlantic world.

Malocello's most concrete achievement was his discovery, or more accurately, his re-discovery and subsequent settlement of one of the eastern Canary Islands, which still bears his Italianized name, Lanzarote. Departing from Genoa, he reached the island around 1312, establishing a trading post and remaining there for approximately two decades, attempting to exploit its resources and convert the indigenous Guanche population. While details of his activities are scarce, his extended presence and the subsequent inclusion of 'Insula de Lanzarotus Marocelus' on Angelino Dulcert's influential 1339 portolan chart confirm the tangible impact of his voyage on European cartography and geographic knowledge, solidifying the archipelago's place on emerging Atlantic maps.
